blocks.text: Imagine your computer running multiple applications smoothly, each believing it has access to a vast memory space. How is this illusion maintained?

blocks.markdown: Virtual memory allows each process to believe it has access to a large, contiguous block of memory, even if the physical memory is much smaller. This is achieved through a combination of hardware and software techniques, primarily involving demand paging and page replacement algorithms.

blocks.title: Virtual Memory
blocks.text: Virtual memory is a memory management capability that provides an 'idealized abstraction of the storage resources' that are actually available on a given machine.

blocks.markdown: When a process accesses a page that is not currently in physical memory, a page fault occurs. The operating system must then load the required page from disk into memory, possibly replacing another page. Let's explore this sequence of events in detail.

blocks.title: Page Fault Sequence
blocks.text:
1. Process attempts to access a page not in physical memory.
2. Hardware traps to the operating system.
3. OS checks if the access is valid and finds a free frame.
4. If no free frame, a page replacement algorithm is used.
5. The required page is read from disk into the frame.
6. Page table is updated.
7. Instruction is restarted.

blocks.markdown: Page replacement algorithms are crucial for managing which pages to keep in memory and which to swap out. We'll examine three common algorithms: FIFO (First-In-First-Out), LRU (Least Recently Used), and Optimal Replacement.

blocks.title: Applying FIFO Replacement
blocks.prompt: Consider a reference string: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, and 3 frames available. Apply FIFO replacement and count the page faults.

steps.text: Process the reference string step-by-step. Replace the oldest page when a new page is needed.
Count page faults: 7, 0, 1 are loaded (3 faults), 2 replaces 7 (4th fault), 0 already in frame, 3 replaces 0 (5th fault), 0 replaces 1 (6th fault), 4 replaces 2 (7th fault), and so on.

blocks.answer: The total number of page faults using FIFO is 9.

blocks.title: Applying LRU Replacement
blocks.prompt: Using the same reference string: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, 2, 3, 0, 3, 2, apply LRU replacement with 3 frames and count the page faults.

steps.text: Process the reference string, replacing the least recently used page when needed.
Count page faults: 7, 0, 1 are loaded (3 faults), 2 replaces 7 (4th fault), 0 already in frame, 3 replaces 1 (5th fault), 0 already in frame, 4 replaces 2 (6th fault), and so on.

blocks.answer: The total number of page faults using LRU is 8.

blocks.markdown: The optimal page replacement algorithm, though impractical for real-time use, serves as a benchmark. It replaces the page that will not be used for the longest period of time in the future.

blocks.title: Thrashing
blocks.text: Thrashing occurs when a system spends more time swapping pages in and out of memory than executing instructions. This can severely degrade performance.

blocks.markdown: The working set model helps to mitigate thrashing by maintaining a set of pages that a process is currently using. If the working set cannot fit in memory, the system may need to reduce the multiprogramming level.

points: Page faults trigger a sequence of events to load pages into memory.
Different page replacement algorithms affect the number of page faults.
Thrashing can be mitigated by managing the working set of pages.
